All summer long, a leaf is green because it's full of chlorophyll.
Chlorophyll catches sunlight and turns it into food for the tree.
When the days get shorter, the tree stops making it.
As the green fades, the yellows and oranges that were there all along start to show.
Some trees also make new red colors in the autumn, which is why maples look like they're on fire.
A few weeks later, the leaves fall, and the tree rests until spring.
Look inside an ordinary door lock, and you'll find a row of tiny pins.
Each pin is split into two pieces, and they come in different lengths.
Springs push the pins down, so they block the cylinder from turning.
When the right key slides in, its ridges lift every pin to exactly the right height.
The splits line up along the edge of the cylinder, and it's free to turn.
The wrong key lifts some pins too far and others not far enough.
That's the whole trick: a handful of pins, and one key that fits them all.
